summary: Introductory discovery between Redwood and Concordia HyperGrid exploring an onramp partnership to route model inference to Concordia's hybrid GPU fabric. Key points: routing policies, VPC peering, throughput/latency targets, security controls (KMS, audit logs), pilot scope (1-week dedicated benchmark), and commercial next steps.
transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2029-11-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Cho (Redwood SE), Ravi Singh (Concordia Head of Partnerships), Elena Moroz (Cloud Architect), Tomas Becker (GPU Eng), Marta Liu (Security)

00:00 Jenna Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jenna from Redwood inference, we have Diego and Lena from our infra / solutions team. How are you all?
00:08 Ravi Singh: Hey Jenna, doing well, thanks. Excited to dig in — we've been chatting a bit over email, wanted to get technical clarity on routing and what an onramp would look like.
00:17 Jenna Park: Great. Quick agenda - run through Concordia's stack and goals, discuss routing options and what we call smart routing / fallback, cover security hoops, and then define a pilot scope. Sound good?
00:28 Elena Moroz: Yep, that's what we need. We'll be honest — we have a hybrid fabric, some hosts in our edge clouds and some in partner colos. Main ask is low-latency routing for specific customers and burst offload for heavy batches.
00:44 Diego Ramos: Cool. Can you give us a quick topology? Are you providing the GPU endpoints as a cloud offering or wanting to interpose routing through Redwood's control plane?
00:52 Tomas Becker: It's both — we want customers to be able to opt to route inference to our Fabric when their provisioning rules match (latency or cost). So Redwood's control plane would decide based on policy. We're exploring either a direct peering or a TLS-forwarding option.
01:10 Lena Cho: When you say peering, is that VPC peering or an API level handshake? We typically do VPC peering for Private but for hosted we have TLS connectors.
01:20 Tomas Becker: VPC peering for enterprise customers; for public tenants we can do a mutually authenticated TLS hop.
01:28 Diego Ramos: Ok that maps to Redwood's deployment modes — hosted API, dedicated pools, and private VPC deployments. For a partner onramp we typically support two path patterns: 1) control-plane routing where Redwood keeps model control and proxies requests to a compatible runtime on a partner side, or 2) a delegated runtime mode where we orchestrate model versions and the partner runs inference natively.
01:52 Ravi Singh: We're leaning to the first initially — Redwood keeps the model and route decisions but sends execution to our GPUs for certain traffic slices. That reduces model sync complexity on our side.
02:03 Diego Ramos: Understood. A couple of clarifying Qs then — what's your expected typical sequence length and request distribution (short chat-ish vs long generation)?
02:11 Elena Moroz: Most customers today are classification / reranking workloads and short chat experiences, 8-64 tokens typical, but we have a few customers doing longer summarization. Peak QPS scenario for our top tenant is about 1.2k rps with 50ms p50 latency targets and p95 around 180-250ms depending on workload.
02:33 Diego Ramos: Thanks. That's helpful. For those latency targets we'll want to look at network egress times, but on the server side we can tune batching and KV cache hits. Also, quantization can help cost but may impact quality.
02:46 Tomas Becker: Quick note — our fabric supports INT8 quantization paths on the newer cards, and we have an FPGA-based preprocessor for tokenization acceleration.
02:54 Lena Cho: Nice. From Redwood's side we have batching, prefix KV cache, and fast path kernels. The routing policy can be per-tenant or per-route with fallbacks. For example, high-priority real-time requests could stay on Redwood's hosted or Dedicated pool; cheaper throughput could route to Concordia for cost savings.
03:18 Ravi Singh: That's the exact flow we want. One concern — SSO, audit logs and KMS integration. Many of our customers require customer-managed keys and an auditable trail of which requests ran on which infra.
03:29 Marta Liu: Right — we need KMS integration, HSM optional, and export controls for logs, plus SOC2 evidence.
03:36 Jenna Park: On the security side we can support KMS integration for keys — Redwood Private has KMS/HSM hooks. For hosted routing we can implement envelope encryption and ensure logs include token-level metadata. We'll send our SOC2 statement and the security whitepaper after the call.
03:52 Elena Moroz: Good. Also wondering about model pinning and version rollouts — if you host the model, how do we ensure reproducible execution and, bucket-wise, are there fallback semantics if our nodes degrade?
04:05 Diego Ramos: We support pinning model versions and rollout policies. If our router detects a capacity issue on the Concordia side we can implement automatic fallback to a Redwood-compatible variant — same model family but maybe slightly different quantization. There's a short window where the KV cache misses may increase.
04:25 Tomas Becker: Cache misses could be tricky for latency — what's the plan for warm starts?
04:30 Lena Cho: We can pre-warm a prefix cache for hot keys, and Redwood has an API for seeding caches when you expect bursts. That plus keep-alives reduces cold start p99.
04:42 Ravi Singh: Makes sense. Let's talk throughput profile — can you do continuous batching but with SLO controls? Some of our customers can't accept large batching that increases p95 beyond 200ms.
04:53 Diego Ramos: Yes, our runtime supports continuous batching with per-route latency SLOs. You can specify max batch sizes, priority windows, and timeouts so critical paths have small batches.
05:06 Elena Moroz: Network-wise, would you prefer us to do a VPC peering in the pilot or start with a mutual TLS egress?
05:12 Jenna Park: For the pilot, mutual TLS is faster to get started and lower friction. For customers that need full private networking and higher throughput we usually transition to VPC peering.
05:23 Tomas Becker: Ok TLS for pilot. For perf testing we'll need a test harness — do you have one?
05:29 Diego Ramos: We have a perf harness and can run benchmarks; but we'd ideally use your real request traces to feed a representative load. If you can share sanitized traces we can run an apples-to-apples benchmark.
05:42 Elena Moroz: We can share anonymized traces. I'll scope a 5-10 minute window that captures peak behavior.
05:49 Diego Ramos: Perfect. That will let us compare Redwood hosted vs Concordia onramp latency and cost per token.
06:00 Ravi Singh: On commercials — we're thinking a revenue share or capacity discount model for certain customers. Do you have standard partner terms?
06:07 Jenna Park: We usually do a couple options — a wholesale rate plus margin, or commit-based reserved capacity for joint customers. For an early pilot we'd propose a trial pricing and then a committed tier. I'll draft a one-pager.
06:20 Ravi Singh: Great. One more technical: how do we handle model compatibility — are there restrictions on which model families can be proxied to your runtime?
06:28 Diego Ramos: In general, transformer-based autoregressive models are supported; for highly custom kernels we may need additional integration. We maintain a model catalog of verified variants and quantization profiles. If you have a custom runtime we can run a short onboarding to create a compatibility profile.
06:45 Tomas Becker: We do have some custom kernels for sparse attention — may need an integration sprint.
06:51 Lena Cho: That would be a technical deep-dive. We can set up a follow-up session specifically for kernel compatibility.
06:58 Marta Liu: Compliance question — do you keep per-request logs in plaintext or redacted, and how long are logs retained by default?
07:05 Jenna Park: By default logs are persisted per our retention policy but can be configured — we can support redaction or shorter retention and export audit logs to your SIEM via syslog/S3. We'll include details in the security pack.
07:18 Elena Moroz: Also, data residency for EU customers — we need processing in eu-central for certain clients. Can routing be region-aware?
07:25 Diego Ramos: Yes, routing rules can be region- and cost-aware. We provide policies that check request metadata and route based on region tags; fallback can be to a regional Redwood pool.
07:36 Ravi Singh: This is helpful. On the pilot scope, proposal idea: one-week dedicated benchmark where Redwood runs canonical model in your test harness, with TLS connector and seeded KV caches. Outcome: performance numbers and a recommended production flow.
07:52 Jenna Park: Sounds good. Diego and I will run the benchmark plan. We'll need sample traces and an SLA target matrix from you.
07:59 Elena Moroz: We'll provide traces and a list of 3 tenant profiles and SLO targets.
08:05 Diego Ramos: Great, we'll also provide a template test plan and measurement scripts.
08:12 Tomas Becker: Any blockers on network NAT traversal or port rules?
08:15 Lena Cho: For TLS mode we just need outbound allowed to Redwood egress endpoints and mutual certs. For VPC peering we'll coordinate CIDR planning.
08:26 Marta Liu: On legal/commercial — we'll want an initial MOU and a set of indemnity clauses around export controls and customer data.
08:33 Jenna Park: We'll route that through Partnerships + Legal. I'll include the MOU skeleton in the follow-up.
08:40 Ravi Singh: Great. I also want to mention potential channel motion — after pilot, we may resell or cross-sell bundled offers to our existing customers.
08:50 Jenna Park: That's interesting — we can explore reseller flows and marketplace listings later.
08:58 Diego Ramos: Quick technical aside — for the benchmark, what's your preferred metric set? We'll collect p50/ p95/ p99 latencies, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens, and cache-hit ratios. Anything else?
09:12 Elena Moroz: RTT to our front door, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory/KV cache hit % would be useful.
09:18 Diego Ramos: Noted. We'll add those.
09:22 Ravi Singh: Ok, I think that covers most. Any final questions from Redwood?
09:26 Lena Cho: Not yet — only to confirm timelines: can we aim to kick the pilot the week of 2029-11-18?
09:33 Elena Moroz: Yes that's feasible.
09:35 Jenna Park: Good. We'll send the checklist and MOU draft by 2029-11-15. Diego will run perf and the benchmark will run 2029-11-18 through 11-24.
09:45 Tomas Becker: We'll prep traces and network creds before then.
09:48 Marta Liu: I'll send compliance items to Jenna by 2029-11-18.
09:52 Jenna Park: Thanks everyone. Quick recap from my side — action items and next steps will be in an email after this call. Any other quick notes?
09:59 Ravi Singh: Nothing else, thanks. Looking forward to the pilot.
10:03 Jenna Park: Thanks all, talk soon.

-- End of meeting --
